THE LATE HON. DANIEL JOHNSON EXPRESSIONS OF REGRET ON PASSING OF QUEBEC PREMIER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the background of our great country is composed of telluric elements of great resistance. Each one of these elements contributes to the strength and personality of our country. From day to day those elements become more obvious, for it will not always be so. From time to time one is tempted to doubt the vigour of the Canadian identity, but in times of distress or of deep reflection, the powerful ties which unite us as Canadians stand out boldly.
Mr. Speaker, one of those ties is the stature of the men who are dedicated to public life in our country. Another tie is the fact that those in power in Canada have always, each in his own way, dedicated themselves to the welfare and the progress of Canada.
It may be said that Canadians have been well served by the men in their public life and that, when one of them passes away, regardless of what part of the country he comes from, it means a loss for the whole country. When a man of Daniel Johnson's stature leaves us, it is not merely the Canadians of that part of the country who are dealt a blow, but Canada as a whole.

Daniel Johnson exemplified those traits which any political leader, or any man, could well choose as standards of measurement: dedication to his country and his province; pride in the achievements and beauty of his culture and its language; courage in the face of adversities both personal and political; calmness and moderation on occasions when a lesser man would have exhibited neither; loyalty to his party and its convictions; devotion to his family.

All Canadians know that our country is going through a period of capital importance
for our future and that the basic values themselves are those which are sometimes questioned when the future is discussed.
There is no doubt that Mr. Daniel Johnson was one of the distinguished participants and interlocutors in that important dialogue which is now going on between Canadians and through which he was trying to find the common values on which the country could agree and unite. We will not forget that his objective was the recognition and the protection of the rights of French Canadians, since that protection is a matter of conscience for all Canadians and it is also, I think, the objective of all good men in Canada.
The people Mr. Johnson represented in the legislature, those who had elected him, those he had served for many years in his riding, know that they could not have a more conscientious, more energetic and, may I say. gracious spokesman.
On behalf of the government of Canada I express my most heartfelt sympathy to his family, to Quebeckers and to the government of Quebec.
Death could not come, Mr. Speaker, at a more untimely moment for this great Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, I was much grieved to hear of the death of Hon. Daniel Johnson.
His friends knew how heavy was his task but we hoped he had completely recovered and was able to resume his duties.
His death is a cruel loss for his family and deprives the country of an experienced and very talented politician. The country loses a man who, even in cases of disagreement at the official level, liked to retain cordial personal relations with the people he met.
He was a gentleman and those who knew him will regret his courtesy, his warmth and his charm.

Tributes to Late Premier Johnson in 1946. He was re-elected six times and served his legislature as deputy speaker and his province as a member of cabinet. It is a good record, sir.

He was premier of Quebec at a time when the evolution of events in that province caused concern in other parts of Canada. It was therefore inevitable that he should be to a certain extent a controversial figure in his country.
I think that, at the present time, a premier of Quebec who loves his people and his country and wants to be loyal to them cannot help but be a controversial figure.
His course was a difficult one, but he followed it with patience and good humour.
He travelled across the country with his family. He wanted to get to know the country as well as he knew the province of Quebec where he was born.
Daniel Johnson wanted to build both Canada and Quebec, and he devoted his life to building a country where all Canadians could fulfil their aspirations.
On behalf of my party as an officer of the House of Commons and personally, because I had the opportunity to work with Premier Daniel Johnson and because I respected and considered him highly, I wish to offer my sincere sympathy to his family, his friends and colleagues as well as to the fellow-citizens of the deceased premier.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Ralliement Credi-tiste I wish to join with the other members of the house to say how we were deeply grieved this morning at the news of the sudden death of Hon. Daniel Johnson, premier of the province of Quebec.
Such a death will be deeply mourned by all the Quebec people and the whole French Canadian nation, and especially by the people of Bagot county, a great part of which is included in Shefford constituency which I have the honour to represent here and which has just lost its member of parliament.
As premier of his province since 1966, and member for Bagot since 1946, he might still, on account of his experience and talent, have served the province of Quebec and all the French Canadian people for many years to come.
In its unfathomable ways Providence has decided that he would no longer be with us after giving yesterday the most eloquent and the most important press conference of his whole political career, as if it were to be the crowning achievement of his work.
September 26, 1968	COMMONS
How forcefully are we reminded of the fragility of life. Although it is full of great possibilities, it is at the same time limited and conditioned by its span and its events.
Mr. Johnson had the courage of his convictions. He had his own disposition, of course. I knew him very well because on many occasions, as members of a good part of the same riding, we presided at the opening of the baseball or hockey season and at the inauguration of sports centres or schools. That is how I came to know the premier of Quebec as a public man and also as a good father.
On television yesterday he said something which impressed me this morning. He said that his illness had made him more human. But today his ailment takes him away from humans and puts an end to his life.
This afternoon he was going to inaugurate the Manicouagan dam which is the most important hydro-electric project in Quebec.
Hon. Maurice Duplessis died in Scheffer-ville, an important mining centre in Quebec. His successor, Hon. Daniel Johnson, died on duty in Manicouagan, an hydro-electric centre in the same Quebec area, in circumstances similar to those which preceded the death of Mr. Duplessis, who liked to look upon Hon. Daniel Johnson as his own son.

Tributes to Late Premier Johnson
History will rate Daniel Johnson as a politician and a statesman who has definitely marked out French Canadian political life. His love of work, his loyalty to his province, his clearsightedness will be missed greatly in Quebec. The strenuous political life which he had set for himself and the responsibilities which he had to assume have unfortunately taken away too soon this dearly beloved father from his family.
On behalf of the Ralliement Creditiste we express our deepest sympathy to Mrs. Johnson, her children and all his relatives, and especially his constituents in the riding of Bagot.
Some of his political enemies might silently rejoice. As far as we are concerned, we share the grief of the whole French Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a statement on wheat. World wheat production in 1968 will likely exceed 10 billion bushels, the third consecutive year in which the 10 billion bushel mark will have been surpassed. This is well above the average of the early 1960's. Competition for export markets will continue to be very keen. During the current crop year, for the period August 1 to September 18, Canadian exports of wheat and flour were 46.7 million bushels as compared with 43.6 million bushels in the same period last year.
Adverse weather conditions in western Canada have delayed the harvest and two weeks of clear warm weather are still required to enable farmers to complete their harvesting operations. Approximately 50 per cent of the crop remains to be harvested at the present time; the grades will be lower this year due mainly to frost and sprouting. The magnitude of the problem associated with handling tough and damp grain will depend a great deal on weather conditions during the next few weeks.
Top priority is being given to the movement of grain from the lakehead terminals to eastern positions for export and domestic use. This movement has been very impressive since the strike ended. During the first ten days of work over half of the 11,863 box cars waiting on track were loaded into the lake-head terminals. This has freed cars for movement from country points, and the movement from country elevators is now proceeding in a more normal fashion.
If there are large quantities of grain with high moisture, the Canadian Wheat Board, the Board of Grain Commissioners and the private grain companies will make every effort to handle such grain from the farmers before it goes out of condition. However, first priority must be given, before the close of navigation, to the movement of clean, dry grain to the lakehead for onward shipment to eastern positions.
As the house is aware, the purpose of the recent Canberra meeting was to review the world wheat situation and the operation of the new international grains arrangement since its entry into force on July 1. The result was positive. Exporter representatives expressed their determination to operate the new arrangement effectively and achieve its objectives, including the observance of the arrangement with respect to minimum prices. Satisfaction was expressed with the operation of the agreement to date and understandings were reached on action to be taken to strengthen the arrangement. It was agreed to fix minimum prices for two Australian hard wheats, and price guide lines were set for certain other wheats not listed in the schedule. New procedures were accepted for the collection of reliable ocean freight information for the calculation of minimum price equivalents and for keeping international wheat prices and export performance under continuing review.
The decisions and recommendations of the Canberra meeting will now be submitted to the prices review committee of the International Wheat Council, which includes representatives of importing countries. This committee will meet in early October, in London. The successful outcome of the Canberra meeting will contribute to price stability for wheat and facilitate the effective implementation of the grains arrangement.
The objective of the government of Canada and the Canadian Wheat Board is to secure 25 per cent of more of world wheat trade. This will mean exports of 1.3 billion bushels in the next three years.
Sales of Canadian wheat are being aggressively promoted on a direct seller to buyer basis. In conjunction with Expo, the Canadian Wheat Board invited all the major wheat buyers from around the world to visit Canada

Recommendations of Canberra Meeting for marketing discussions and tours of our grain facilities. These visits aroused a great deal of interest and are now being followed up by Canadian Wheat Board missions into overseas markets wherever a sales potential exists.

I have written personally to senior trade commissioners of each of my department's offices abroad to ensure that no sales opportunity is overlooked. They are to submit market development suggestions based on their on-the-spot experience.
Private grain companies in their position as agents for the Canadian Wheat Board have a vast network of overseas contacts and are vigorously pursuing all export opportunities.
Individual sales on credit terms are being negotiated and I expect that the extension of credit arrangements by the government will result in the conclusion of significant sales in the near future. The government continues to purchase substantial quantities of wheat and flour for Canada's food aid program.
In order to mobilize more effectively the energies and experience of associations and organizations directly concerned with wheat exports, the government will establish, as a matter of priority, a national grains council. The Minister of Agriculture and I will be meeting with the interested groups in Winnipeg on October 16 to discuss the scope of the council's membership, its organization, administration, and terms of reference.
As I stated earlier, our objective is to export 1.3 billion bushels of wheat during the next three years. We are determined to do that or better.
In conclusion, the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Lang) and I are collaborating closely on all these matters. He will shortly be introducing legislation to double the level of cash advances for grain producers. Together with our colleague, the Minister of Agriculture, and with the help of the national grains council, we shall be addressing ourselves urgently and intently to both the short and long term problems and opportunities for the Canadian grain industry. The grain economy of Canada is a matter of national interest. Success in our production and sales policies and performance is a major factor in Canadian prosperity from east to west.

At the outset I might say we are happy that at long last the government recognizes the situation to be a serious one. I agree that western Canada is encountering serious difficulties from the point of view of climate. But farmers have faced bad weather before. The most serious problem which faces western Canada arises from the fact that when the international wheat agreement was negotiated by the former government-and many of the ministers responsible are members of the present administration-the negotiating team did not reach the conference at Geneva on time. In our opinion, and in the opinion of many experts in the agriculture field, the farmers of Canada were shortchanged in this regard. Before the agreement was approved by the various parliamentary institutions and governments of the exporting and marketing nations, the United States, a business country with a large surplus, dumped her grain on many of Canada's traditional markets.
This situation is the most serious which western farmers have faced since 1956 when approximately 700 million bushels of wheat were piled up on the farms and in the elevators. Crops are above average in most parts and quotas are very low-practically negligible. Financing is hard to come by at this time of the year and as a result farmers are having difficulty in meeting their obligations. Young farmers especially, who just entered the trade within the last few years, are unable to meet their mortgage payments, and if it were not for provincial legislation in Alberta and Saskatchewan foreclosure would be the letter of the day. Therefore I must say that on the shoulders of the government rests the responsibility for the fall-off in markets.
Members of the government can bring in new legislation which is commendable in reference to increasing the cash advances, and which will temporarily relieve the situation. On that matter I congratulate them, but the fact remains that the grain trade will not become healthy unless farmers are able to sell their commodities; and the loss of markets is the responsibility of the government.
Since the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) has said that the spokesman for western agriculture is now the Minister without Portfolio from Saskatchewan (Mr. Lang), together with the Minister of

As the Winnipeg Free Press has pointed out, the main thing is to export grain. Many critics are talking about a two-price system, but that would not mean very much to the western farmer because domestically we consume approximately only 50 million bushels in Canada, including some domestic consumption for feed stock. Therefore if we introduced a two-price system, as suggested by some experts, providing another nickel a bushel for exports, it would not help the western farmer very much. It is the responsibility of the government to find markets, and I repeat that the responsibility for the loss of those markets lies directly on the shoulders of some of the ministers who sit in the government.

There is always a railway transportation problem for the eastern farmers, as the minister has stressed.
In 1962, in this house, I asked that grain elevators be built and transportation made by water. Everyone welcomed the suggestion that the waterways should be used to help the eastern farmers but, although the Liberals have succeeded the Conservatives, the problem has not been solved yet and today the question is how to move western grain to the eastern farmers. The farmers would pay much less by water and greater consumption would result, if the farmers did not have to leave their farms.

I hope, therefore, that this affluence will be distributed throughout the world, after the problem has been solved in Canada, so that this plenty which God allows will not be a punishment but a blessing for all the Christians of the world.

Mr. Speaker, I have a statement regarding certain changes in the operations of the Post Office. The Post Office Department in its continuing study of the requirements of the various services has reached the conclusion that a number of changes should now be made. The increased costs of labour, supplies and transportation has added substantially to the cost of operating the Post Office Department. We consider that the department must operate within the limits of the revenue produced. The contemplated changes will produce a substantial reduction in the cost of operating the department.
Our studies have indicated that several services are no longer required to the same extent as in the past. Business firms generally are operating on shorter hours and on a five day week. There is not, therefore, the same need to provide postal service on week ends when most businesses are closed. I should like to remark here that approximately 80 per

cent of all first class mail originates in business and in government. It is, therefore, intended to close the post offices on Saturdays. Deliveries of mail will not be made on Saturdays. This will include letter carrier service, parcel post and rural route deliveries. Special delivery service will continue to be provided on a seven day week basis. Mail will continue to be processed and forwarded to destinations over the week end in order to be available for delivery on Monday. Mailings are generally very light on Saturdays and Sundays and this essential work can be carried on by a minimum staff.
In order to provide the means to purchase stamps on Saturdays, sub post offices which are operated in connection with retail outlets which are open on Saturdays, will remain open. A program to instal additional stamp vending machines will also be undertaken.
These changes, which are scheduled for implementation on February 1, 1969 will provide a much more desirable work week for the majority of postal employees. These changes represent significant improvements in working conditions and we are convinced they will be readily acceptable by the majority of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I may say at the outset that this is a somewhat casual way of announcing the diminution in the service of one of the great public utilities of this country. I note the minister is announcing on a week end that in effect the postal services will be operated on a five day week. Let me reflect further on the merits of the case.
I should like to say in passing that it is regrettable that the traditional courtesy extended in the house of allowing opposition members to have a gander at statements of ministers is not being followed. I have some difficulty in dealing with what the minister has just said. I noted his reference to the closing of some sub post offices and the retention of service in some others. It would strike me that, according to the dissertation that he has just made, he might be in danger of having the jurisdiction in effect, in relation to the service to be rendered, geared to another authority rather than the government of Canada. I think these matters must be looked at with great care.
It is also my belief that the whole subject might have been introduced in a less casual way, so that the matter at this initial stage could have been reflected upon by the people

I can promise that in the future we shall have more to say about this matter. At this time we have no reason to believe that there is not a good deal of merit in the suggestion. We do want to see improved facilities for the workers in our post offices, but we do not want any detriment to the service to our public.

Mr. Speaker, I join with the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) in expressing some amazement at the casual way in which a long standing practice in this country can be changed simply by a government announcement. It does seem to me that, with an item in the name of the Postmaster General on the order paper, which means that in due course we will be discussing matters affecting this department, there might have been a discussion in the House of Commons about this proposal before it was brought into effect.
The Postmaster General has made some pretty categorical statements about the extent to which businesses are on a five day week. It strikes me that he has been a bit rigid in what he has said, and that parliament ought to have had the opportunity to consider the position of those who may require service over the week end. I would point out that the suggestion that special delivery service will still be available on Saturday and Sunday is a way of saying that if people must have service on week ends, which they have been used to over the years, they will have to pay higher rates.
As the hon. member for Hillsborough suggested, there is undoubtedly merit in the idea of streamlining and making changes. We should not be people who say that because something has always been done, that is the way it should always be done. However, it does strike me as a bit alarming that we are beginning to get this succession of announcements on a unilateral basis from the government benches as to changes that are going to be made.
We had one from the Prime Minister a couple of days ago that we did not like. Now we have one from the Postmaster General. Who next without prior discussion, is going to stand up and tell parliament what is going to be done? As I have already said, there is an item on the order paper which we will reach in due course. I hope that when we reach it,

Mr. Speaker, first I wish to tell the minister that we are glad of his endeavours to rejuvenate the Post Office Department and make it more efficient. In his report dated September 27, 1965, Justice Anderson made the following comments:

Mr. Speaker, the estimates which were tabled the other day obviously make it clear that expenses which are not controllable by the government have risen beyond any expectation. It is obvious that we cannot break a statute or an agreement which has been reached with the provinces, and that these expenses have exceeded everyone's expectations. We have tried to compensate for that by cutting very seriously into all the controllable expenditures. Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to propose any amendment or to withhold the granting of interim supply. Still, in the circumstances there are a number of things I feel impelled to say to the committee.
One must begin with the estimates tabled by the President of the Treasury Board a few days ago, and with the statement that the minister made in tabling them. The revised estimates presented to the house amount to some $10,670 million for the current fiscal year, more than $400 million higher than what we were assured by the government on various occasions would be the maximum. In other words, the estimates now tabled exceed the commitment given by the government by some $400 million.
We must consider the circumstances that prevailed when these assurances were given over a period of time. Last winter the government was in a state of financial and political crisis. One must recall that in the last fiscal year the government was operating at a deficit of some $800 million and that last autumn, almost a year ago, the then minister of finance and the then president of the treasury board, as a result of concern about inflation, began to be concerned about the size of the deficit and began talking about cuts in estimates for the year in which we now find ourselves.
Hon. members who were here in the house at that time will recall the talk of hon. gentlemen opposite about the cutting they were doing to the extent of some $650 million, I think, on estimates not yet presented to the
[Mr. Drury.l
house. Of course this was exposed as the phony claim it was since it was nothing more than the normal process of a government cutting back on estimates presented to it by departments. Nevertheless this was the beginning of a series of assurances given to the house and the country by the then minister of finance and the then president of the treasury board.
Eventually estimates were presented for the present fiscal year, and in accordance with statements made previously by the then minister of finance and the then president of the treasury board the total of these estimates was just under $10,300 million without any provision for medicare or write-off of the Expo deficit. The then minister of finance also proposed certain tax increases, and the budget was discussed on the basis of those estimates and those tax proposals.
In the month of February the roof more or less fell in on the government. A severe financial crisis developed, including a severe drain on the Canadian dollar, and this provoked further assurances from the then minister of finance and the then minister in charge of the treasury board in order to ease the minds of the gnomes of Zurich as well as the Canadian people. Further assurances were given, including a reduction of some $75 million more from the estimates.
Let us have no mistake, Mr. Chairman, as to what the firm commitment of the government was. The firm commitment was a ceiling of $10,225 million on estimates for the current year, although at that time I think the minister of finance of the day still made an exception with regard to medicare and the writeoff in connection with Expo. However, as matters developed, further assurances were made during the election campaign, in the course of selling a Canadian bond issue in the amount of some $100 million in the United States. A further assurance was given involving the honour and the good faith of Canada.
In the prospectus filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, which I referred to this morning in a question to the Prime Minister, a prospectus signed by the Minister of Finance who I am sorry is not in the chamber, it was stated that it was intended to reduce expenditures further to a level of $10,225 million without qualification, even dropping the qualification relating to medicare and the write-off of Expo. This was a firm commitment in the prospectus filed with the S.E.C., which went on to say that this would

bring the budgetary position for the fiscal year 1969 very close to a balance.
When the President of the Treasury Board tabled the revised estimates the other day he tried, rather skilfully, I thought, to give the impression, without saying so, that the government was living up to any commitment it had given because it had made, as it promised to do, a cut of $75 million, indeed, a little more, in the estimates over which it had control. Let there be no mistake, Mr. Chairman. The commitment made by the government was with regard to total estimates without qualification, and the revised estimates tabled in the house the other day by the minister violated that commitment to the extent of more than $400 million.
Last winter the assurances given by the then minister of finance were that the increase in expenditures this fiscal year over last would be held to about 4 per cent. In fact, according to the revised estimates it is about 8 per cent, which is just 100 per cent wrong, Mr. Chairman.
Shame.

Post-secondary education is another. I think we would all agree that it would be a very serious mistake if this program were cut back. It would be a very serious mistake for the future of hundreds of thousands of Canadians and the country as a whole. So far as the Canada Assistance Plan is concerned, I think the approach has to be much broader than apparently the government has in mind. I believe the government has to think in terms of an overhaul of its whole anti-poverty program and should seek a new approach rather than the one suggested, which is just an attempt to place ceilings on the program now in effect.
Then there is the subject of medicare. I say in all sincerity that if the government feels it is necessary to review-and I do not criticize this; I see their problem-the rapidly escalating costs of existing shared cost programs, is not this the time to heed the request of the provinces to confer about the medicare program? Is not this the last chance the government really has to exercise some control over the escalation of the cost of shared cost programs?
I think the provinces sincerely want a medicare program. Most of them have indicated that they do not really like the present one; they are concerned about the effect it has on their other priorities. The government of Canada seems to be seriously concerned about the strait-jacket in which existing shared cost programs are placing them. If the government considers this to be the time to review existing shared cost programs, is this not all the more reason to meet the provinces and talk seriously about the medicare program? This may be the last chance the government has to keep this country out of a serious strait-jacket.
There were a good many other things that I wanted to say. The difficulty in which the Leader of the Opposition now finds himself is that there are so many things to be said against the government, and I do not wish to trespass too much upon the good nature of the house. But I will say that this parliament is only two weeks old, the government has been in office for about five months, and there is still time to change. There is still time for the government to pull itself together and begin to deal frankly and responsibly with parliament and the country.
And honestly.

I have spent some time this morning developing one aspect of this matter, the lack of frankness of the government and the secrecy running through the whole fabric of the government. There is still time to break out of the financial strait-jacket in which the government believes it is. There is still time for the Prime Minister to call a halt here and now to the uncertainty and confusion growing about the policies of the government and their sense of commitment.
What is the impression given by the government? As I indicated this morning, they are certainly not committed to frankness. They seem to be committed neither to the monarchy nor to republicanism, neither to the parliamentary nor the congressional system of government. They seem to be fully committed neither to collective security nor to withdrawal from NATO. Certainly the government is not committed to compassion either at home or abroad. It has abandoned the anti-poverty program, and we express serious concern about the government's lack of concern with regard to Biafra.
The government has no commitment to excellence in Canada. It has cut down on science programs, on research and even on the arts. There is uncertainty in the country about the government's determination to play a part in western defence. There is uncertainty on the part of Canadians about whether we can expect the government to translate into action what we have always thought were Canada's ideals of compassion as well as justice for people. There is uncertainty in the scientific community and universities about whether the government takes seriously the need for scientific development in Canada. There is uncertainty about what has taken place in the discussions regarding the constitution.
There is a growing feeling in Canada that the government has no real sense of commitment. This being the case, let this chamber demonstrate that we have a sense of commitment. Let us encourage the government to courageously break out of its financial morass. Let the committees on external affairs and national defence draw up a program that could provide some relief, even at this late hour, to Biafra. Let the committee make its own assessment of Canada's role in NATO. Let the appropriate committee give the government a sense of priority so they may establish priorities in these fields. Let us have a committee study the constitution. Let us involve members of this house in the vital
September 27, 19S8

work of achieving a national consensus. That is what we are here for. Let the government appoint a committee of this house, or of the Senate and House of Commons, to study the question of poverty.
Before this house met the Prime Minister promised the country that this would be a jumping place. It looks like a jumping-off place for the government. But let us make it a jumping place. If there is no sense of commitment on the part of the government, let those of us in the opposition, those on the back benches on this side of the house, demonstrate that parliament and its members do have a sense of commitment, a sense of conviction and a sense of compassion.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention to follow the arguments put forward this morning by the Leader of the Opposition, but I am sure we shall all await with interest a possible reply from the government to the points that he made. However, I do wish that when Liberals and Conservatives discuss this question of government expenditure they would look at it in terms other than just amounts of money and whether these amounts are higher or lower than were predicted. It seems to us that what really counts when you are dealing with government expenditures is the way those expenditures are made and the way in which taxes are levied for the collection of the necessary revenue.
We are concerned, of course, about economy. We do not wish to see unnecessary expenditure and we think waste should be squeezed out. However, our main concern about government expenditures is that they be directed toward making life secure and just for the people of this country. We think that is the purpose of government programs, that money spent on them, unlike much of the money that is spent in the private sector, is an investment in people. We want to see a further development of government programs which make it possible for people to have
Interim Supply
decent incomes, decent homes, adequate education and social security. We are not fazed by statements such as the Prime Minister made this morning when he suggested that the opposition asks for lower expenditures and at the same time for more programs. We think it is the business of the government to set up programs for the good of the people of the country, and we recognize that they have to be paid for.
The other side of the coin, as I have already suggested, is the manner in which government revenues are collected. We think that collection should be on as fair a basis as possible, that taxes, fundamentally, should be levied on the basis of ability to pay. There are details in the Carter report with which we may not agree, but in the main we regard it as an excellent document advancing the idea that taxes can be collected according to ability to pay, and also advancing the proposition that wealth should not escape taxation to the extent that is the case in this country. As I say, we get a little tired of these altercations back and forth between the government and the official opposition over the amount that the budget or the estimates may reach. What is important to us is the things on which the money is spent and the fairness of the taxation methods by which it is collected. We find both of the major parties deficient on both these counts.
I do not intend to elaborate any further on that aspect of the matter, but there is one other general comment I would like to make and then there are a couple of details to which I wish to refer. I may say that one or two of my colleagues also have some matters of detail about which they will be speaking later this afternoon.
The general comment I wish to make-and I am glad for this purpose to have the ear of my friend, the President of the Privy Council-is that I think the exercise in which we are engaged today demonstrates once again how urgent it is for us to review the methods by which we vote supply. Today we are being asked for roughly nine-twelfths of the year's estimates. The resolution is set up in such a way that it takes cognizance of the interim supply which was voted in the old parliament last March. It also takes cognizance of the fact that the government lived on Governor General's warrants for several months during the period of the election and thereafter. But the fact is that this motion not only covers all those months of expenditures which were not discussed in detail but goes on to provide supply for October, November and December.

September 27, 1368
Interim Supply
In other words, when this debate is over and we have passed the interim supply bill we will have approved nine-twelfths or 75 per cent of the year's expenditures without-and I say this quite frankly-any discussion in detail of the expenditures themselves.
[DOT] (2:40 p.m.)
We had the opportunity of making speeches on interim supply last March and we have the opportunity of making speeches today on matters of policy or on issues about which we are concerned. But if we keep this up for the whole 19 days that we have allotted ourselves for discussion of the 1968-69 estimates and supply at this session, we still will not get around to an examination, in any kind of detail, of the estimates that are before us.
I have been here for quite a few years now, Mr. Chairman, and cannot remember a session when we really did this kind of job and went into the details of the expenditures to ascertain whether or not they were correct, whether or not they were valid, whether or not they should be cut down or increased. We just do not use our supply days for that purpose. We use the days and we use the items as pegs for making speeches about matters that we think are important.
I do not deprecate what we are doing, Mr. Chairman. I do not downgrade it at all. I think it is important. It is an opportunity to get up on the floor of the house and deal with issues that we think are alive and current. However, in the process of doing this the job of critically examining the estimates just is not done by the House of Commons. It has been done in advance by Treasury Board. In a year or two from now it will be done by the public accounts committee after the Auditor General has made his report.

What I say now is not by way of castigating anybody. I am not assessing the blame. But unless there is some new machinery of a sort we have not had during the quarter of a century that I have been connected with this house. I do not see estimates being adequately discussed on the floor of the House of Commons. We have too much to do.

Even if we were to spend a whole year examining the billions of dollars of estimates, Mr. Chairman, we still would not do the job. The officials are not here for questioning, and the ministers are not as bright about these things as we might wish them to be. Perhaps they are not as bright-period. Surely the case becomes stronger every year for a reference of the estimates to committees that have the time and the research assistants to enable them to do the job properly. Otherwise, Mr. Chairman, we might as well give up the notion that in parliament we have any control over the pursestrings. The only control that is really exercised is by Treasury Board; and this morning the Leader of the Opposition wanted to fire the staff of Treasury Board. Then where would we be?
Therefore I plead that we take this matter pretty seriously. Someone may throw this back to me and tell me that I am one of those likely to be on the committee on procedure and that is the place for us to consider this problem. But, Mr. Chairman, we need the backing and the desire of the house for new machinery to do the job, a job that certainly has not been done for a great many years.
Total government expenditures for the year 1968-69 as at last report-they may go up again before the year ends-are in the order of $10,670 million, of which $5,780 million require to be voted. The rest of the money is provided by statute. By the time we get through with the exercise in which we are engaged today and include the interim supply that we voted last March, we will have voted $4,894 million out of that $5,784 million that is before us for this fiscal year without discussing any of the details at all.
In terms of examining the estimates, Mr. Chairman, this exercise is nothing but a farce. I do not say that debating interim supply is a farce. I think that having supply days when we raise issues such as that which the Leader of the Opposition felt he had to raise this morning and that other hon. members will raise this afternoon is all to the good. We are making good use of our time and I defend it. But the job that we talk about doing, examining the estimates, is just not being done by members of parliament anywhere at any time. I hope that the exercise we are going through today, will demonstrate the importance of the job that the procedure committee has to do, namely, to bring back some suggestions as to the ways and means of handling supply.
September 27, 1968

I said, Mr. Chairman, that while I was on my feet there were a couple of detailed matters to which I wanted to make reference. They are items that came up this morning. I am sorry that the ministers concerned do not happen to be here at the moment, but they may wander in. Maybe this is not the day that they do not have to be here.
This morning I asked the Minister of Transport about the Air Canada overhaul and maintenance base at Winnipeg. In particular I asked him whether there was anything to reports that Air Canada is considering selling that base to a private firm, one of several being mentioned in press reports. I also asked him whether this matter was under consultation with the unions of the employees who work for Air Canada at Winnipeg.
I must say that I was not at all satisfied with his answer. The minister's answer confirms that something is in the wind. He said that the report was speculative, but it looked like pretty solid speculation by the time he got through his answer. I had to press him a second time to answer the question whether or not the unions concerned are being consulted, and in effect he said that they know what is going on and that he will bring them into the picture just before the last documents are signed.
This is not good enough, Mr. Chairman. This is not participatory democracy. This is not involvement-and you remember that word, Mr. Chairman. The Prime Minister did not make many speeches during the last election campaign and the ones that he did make were pretty short. But the word "involvement" got into every one of them. This is what this great new political force was up to-getting the people of Canada involved in the running of their affairs. One of the affairs that affects people most of all is their work.
We suggest, Mr. Chairman, that if democracy means anything and if involvement means anything, the employees who work for Air Canada at Winnipeg should have some say if changes are being contemplated which put them into a position where they either have to pull up stakes and leave Winnipeg, as so many others have had to do, or transfer their employment from a crown corporation for which they have been glad to work to a private corporation for which they may not be so pleased to work. I urge the Minister of Transport not to think that he can satisfy us by saying that the unions will be told just before the ink is dry on the final signatures. They should be in the picture now in terms of the involvement which the Prime Minister
Interim Supply
said would be the key to public affairs in this country.

Later he said aid might be sent to all the needy persons, but it could not be sent to everyone. I should like to see what the priorities are that rate before the needs of the Biafra people. That is not the attitude of a government filled with the spirit of humani-tarianism as voiced by the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
What are you going to do about the situation? The members of the opposition have pressed for action. What answer did we get again today? We received a cynical shrug and the answer that nothing can be done. Weeks ago we told the government to try to bring this matter before the United Nations and we were told that could not be done because the government did not know how to draft a resolution that would be humanitarian. It didn't want a political resolution, but for God's sake, will this government act now when thousands are dying? The answer we receive is that the government must be careful because 27 African states believe that this is an internal affair. These are most of the African states to which we are giving aid. Are we giving this aid, as suggested, to undermine the relationship between them and the republic of France?
The Prime Minister had an interview, program no. 51-22103-8001, and he was asked about this question. He said:
-it wasn't my purpose to try and achieve any awards for the Speech from the Throne or from my speech in the debate. That's not the object of government, is it, to get bleeding hearts or purple hearts,-
He finally ended up in the course of that interview by saying this:
Well I'd like to discuss it with you, Mr. Lynch. I would like to discuss it with the Canadian people because my heart bleeds as much as anyone else's when I know that people are starving. But there

have been civil wars before, and the question is, once again, that the African states decide that this thing is an internal question.
He went on to say that if we act we will have our planes shot down. Why will Canada not act by placing a motion before the United Nations? If the other nations will not join Canada, we will at least have given the lead to the world by saying that this is wrong.
Why is there this unimaginative diffidence to act? Sometime the government will have to act, perhaps when these people over there are all dead. Perhaps then this government will step in and say it will put a resolution before the United Nations. I suggest in all seriousness that something should be done now. I agree that the government cannot do everything and may not get such a resolution through but at least if it tries, Canada will be taking a stand which it has not taken up to now. All the elusive evasiveness of saying that we have sent over quite a bit to Lagos, and we are sure that somebody is getting it, does not help. There is no way that we can force the government to act on a matter like this. I do not know who is the acting minister or the acting acting minister of external affairs, but I take it-what is his portfolio-it is the Minister of Industry and so on. He said: Mr. Speaker, I am reintroducing this bill. It was originally put forward by the then hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard on February 25, 1966. thinks this should be brought about. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO EXTEND APPLICATION TO PROFESSIONAL SPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to support this excellent bill, No. C-2, to amend the Combines Investigation Act to include professional sports within the purview of the act. I foresee very good prospects for its ultimate success, because the history of this measure is that it is supported by at least three of the parties represented here. It was introduced by a member of the government, the then hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard, on two previous occasions, as Bill No. C-132 in 1966 and as Bill No. C-99 in 1967. Also, as we have just heard, the bill was introduced by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis). Therefore, it apparently enjoys the almost unanimous support of this house.
As a member from a riding in the greater Vancouver area, I have a particular reason for being sensitive about the way professional sports franchises are awarded. This is not only because recently, in spite of substantial federal and local investment in the most modern sports facilities in Canada, the $6 million Coliseum in Vancouver, that city has twice been turned down by the N.H.L. in Its request
DEBATES	535
Combines Investigation Act for a major hockey league franchise. The reason given originally for this refusal was that Vancouver had no suitable rink. This reason is no longer pertinent. The specific reason for the latest refusal escapes me at the moment, but I think it revolved around the proposed ownership of the team and the franchise applicants, who were somehow undesirable.
We of Vancouver also recall that some 15 years ago our first request to have a Canadian football league franchise was rebuffed. Our subsequent application was successful. However, I will not dwell or elaborate upon B.C.'s professional football team. In any event, hockey fans where I live are being denied the opportunity-and I quote from the bill-to participate or observe professional hockey as it applies to the major league. Some people where I live are unkind enough to say that the lower mainland people cannot watch first-rate hockey because a three-way split of television revenue would obtain, instead of the present rather comfortable Toronto-Montreal arrangement of lucrative television proceeds.
The former hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, now the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, had this to say when introducing his bill in 1966. I shall not read the same portion of his remarks as was read by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. Further down on page 1779 of Hansard for February 25, 1966, the then hon. member for Vancou-ver-Burrard is reported as having said:
While this amendment includes all professional sports it is immediately directed at the National Hockey League whose president, Mr. Clarence Campbell, has made it clear that its owners are interested only in their own welfare and not the public interest.
I am certain that members of my party would agree wholeheartedly, as I do, with this statement. Since it was pointed out previously that the matter of combines legislation comes under the direct authority of the hon. member who previously introduced the bill, the now Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the amendment before us should proceed with the speed of lightning.
This is a very fortunate private member's bill indeed, Not only was it originally sired by the minister directly concerned, but it has been adopted by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, and I would be pleased to act as its godfather. But if this were not enough, at least two other ministers of the Crown have spoken in positive terms about the sentiments expressed in the bill. On
September 27, 1963

Combines Investigation Act June 4, 1967, the then registrar general, now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), was reported in the Toronto Star as follows:
Ottawa to rule 'pro' sports Turner says.
Registrar General John Turner said in the commons yesterday the government intends to put professional sport under the regulation of federal authority.
The article further says:
He said he hoped the Combines Investigation Act can be amended soon to include professional sport.
Today, an official in the combines branch revealed that the government move was touched off by Vancouver's failure to get a National Hockey League franchise. When the N.H.L. doubled in size this year by adding six teams, the new franchises went to U.S. cities.
One year later, on June 4, 1968, the government re-emphasized its position when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated during an election campaign visit to Selkirk college in Castlegar, British Columbia.
"The federal government must do more for sports," he said. New N.H.L. franchises have gone entirely to the United States instead of partly to Canada, while U.S. baseball's national league has awarded a franchise to Montreal.
Every major Canadian city is entitled to an N.H.L. team, the Prime Minister said.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
It appears then that we have what amounts to an all party agreement that professional sport is indeed a big business and that clearly it belongs within the regulatory conditions of the Combines Investigation Act.
There is one other aspect of the bill to which I wish to turn my attention for a moment, and that is the phrase "restrict the opportunity of Canadians to participate in". I should like to put the emphasis on the words "to participate in" professional sports because I believe that it expresses the personal freedom aspect of the bill as opposed to the public interest aspect which I have just discussed.
With the growth of television sport programs and the attendant commercialism, an inverse relationship is developing whereby major leagues are growing at the expense of the minor leagues. In the short run there are fewer opportunities for athletes to earn their living by doing things they do best and like to do best.
Since there are fewer opportunities for professional athletes to learn their trade in independently owned minor leagues and teams, there is a consequent limiting of a player's freedom to sell his services to his own best economic advantage. Particularly pernicious is the current vertical integration

of the sports industry which allows an "owned" player to be consigned to the minor leagues-on occasions permanently and without his consent-at a time when other major leagues could use him and he would like to play for them. This is feudalism of the worst possible kind and a direct invasion of the rights and freedoms of an individual.
The Carl Brewer amateur reinstatement case was a recent example of the power of the N.H.L. owners, but most fans will remember how early attempts at forming a hockey players union-a right now given freely to other citizens in an enlightened age-were crushed by the moguls.
Questions about players' contracts have been raised repeatedly in this house, so it is not a matter of small concern or even a new one to the people of Canada. Just over a year ago the N.H.L. governors finally accepted, after a difficult fight, a players association, not a union but a fairly innocuous sounding thing called an association, to fight for players' rights and contracts.
The fight is far from won, and that is why we need to pass this bill as it is, paying special attention to the phrase "the right to participate in professional sports" for the sake of the individual athlete. I am not speaking now of the star or the exception, but rather of the average athlete whose professional life is exceedingly brief-it is even worse than a politician's-and much of whose time must be devoted to his profession so that often little time is left over for him to prepare for another career when his playing days are over.
In conclusion, I want to make two points. There are powerful lobbies constantly at work both here and in the United States to exempt professional sport from the anti-trust legislation. Over the years the U.S. congress, especially in the 1950s, has been bombarded to exempt professional baseball, football and hockey from the anti-trust legislation, and many attempts have nearly succeeded. In 1961, the sale of television rights was exempted. Senate judiciary committees in the United States have made anti-trust recommendations relating to sport. I cite these cases to indicate that a large section of the people in the United States and their elected representatives have had reason to believe that professional sport is a big business, a virtual monopoly, and needs greater public control.
The final point I would like to make in support of the bill is to say that I think we can take one further step along the road to
September 27, 1S68	COMMONS
encourage greater interest and accomplishment in Canada's young athletes and thereby stimulate Canadian pride inspired by such people as Barbara Ann Scott, Harry Jerome, Nancy Green and Jean Belliveau. "Champions", says Nancy, "provide the impetus to get people participating at the grass roots level".
I commend the bill as a measure to bring champions and major sports to more people in Canada sooner, to encourage our athletes to stay in Canada and to receive recognition by playing for Canadian teams before live Canadian audiences. May I also remind hon. members of the statement made by the Minister of Health and Welfare on August 14, as reported in the Toronto Star, when speaking about the new sport task force when he said "I can't really see how the franchises come within the terms of reference".
I am certain that this bill will ensure that individual and public interests are well cared for. I, therefore, believe we should pass the bill with all possible haste.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I admire the desire and the attempt of the mover and seconder of the bill to break the hold of these so-called sports barons over their athletic serfs, or to put it another way, to loosen their tentacles from the youthful players in the hockey farm systems,
I must speak against the bill because in my opinion it is not possible to accomplish the desired result by a public bill. Nor do I believe it is wise to consider a sport amendment to the Combines Investigation Act at a time the whole field to which the act relates is under intensive study and review.
Since February 29, 1966, the date referred to by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Maclnnis), this is what has happened. In July, 1966, the late Hon. Guy Favreau, former president of the privy council and the minister then responsible for the administration of the act, announced that the whole subject of consumer affairs, including combines and restraint of trade, was being referred to the economic council for a comprehensive review and for a report. He also said that any amendment to the legislation should be in keeping with the fundamental philosophy of the act and that it would be unwise to enact temporary or piecemeal amendments.
In March of 1968 the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner), then minister of consumer and corporate affairs, stated in the house that the prohibitions in the Combines Investigation
DEBATES	537
Combines Investigation Act Act did not cover the service factor of the business community under which sports would be classified but related only to articles which could be the subject of trade or commerce, their transportation, storage or rental. He also asserted the desirability of obtaining a possible new jurisdiction, namely civil jurisdiction, for enforcement of the act under the trade and commerce head of section 91 of the British North America Act. At that time he pointed out that the specific subject, as referred to the economic council, was still under consideration by them.
The director of investigation and research, under the act, in his report tabled in the house, stated that a research study into service industries, at present not within the scope of the act, including professional sports, was in progress. At present, parliamentary authority to legislate in this area rests upon jurisdiction in the criminal law field. Because of the nature of the enforcement, the act appears criminal in purpose. However, it is well recognized that at least to date the purpose of the legislation is an economic one, namely, to provide competitive behaviour and thus to maintain free and open competition as a stimulus to the optimum use of resources in a free enterprise system.
It may very well be that the economic council may find a concurrent basis for authority under the trade and commerce head of section 91 of the B.N.A. Act which would then allow civil enforcement. In my opinion it would be much better if those entrusted with the enforcement of the act had the alternative of proceeding by civil action, leaving to criminal proceedings only the most flagrant violations.
In a criminal prosecution, the proposed indictment usually goes before a grand jury which can throw it out, and sometimes does. If the grand jury allows the matter to proceed, a criminal trial follows. The criminal process is long and expensive. Quite often the prosecution is not successful because the issues are numerous and complicated and the onus of proof is heavy in a criminal case.
While I was acting for the prosecution in a case under the Combines Investigation Act, I was struck by the time and expense necessary to prepare to prove all the details required in this type of criminal prosecution. I expressed the view at that time, and do so again, that breaches of the act could, in most cases, be dealt with more efficiently and with less expense in a civil action.
September 27, 1968

Combines Investigation Act [DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
What are the advantages, Mr. Speaker, of proceeding in a civil action? First, there is an examination for discovery, which is like a pre-trial examination of the other side under oath. At this time admissions can be obtained as to the great majority of the facts and all of the documents are produced and admitted. This would narrow the issue and reduce the number of witnesses at trial. This in turn would cut the length of trial and expense. For years these lengthy proceedings under the Combines Investigation Act, proceeding as they have on a criminal basis, have been congesting our courts and slowing the judicial process. The average length of time for one of these proceedings is from one to two months.
One might ask how a civil procedure could be effective when we cannot provide for punishment by fine, as in a criminal case. We must remember, however, that in civil proceedings we have the injunction or restraining order which is most effective. If, after the injunction is granted, the breach of the act continues, an application can be made to have the directors and officers of the corporation committed to jail or fined for contempt of court. This can be far more effective in enforcing the act than a fine against the corporation, which is usually paid out of the corporate treasury and does not cause any hurt to the person who caused the offence. Further, in a civil case the offending corporation would be required to pay the legal costs of the proceedings against it, which in many cases would exceed the amount of the average fine imposed.
Another possibility is the consideration of the American system where an independent commission issues a cease and desist order, leaving it up to the alleged offender to show that the order should not stand.
Section 32 of the act to which the proposed amendment would be attached, and under which most of the prosecutions are brought, reads as follows:
(1) Every one who conspires, combines, agrees or arranges with another person:
(a)	to limit unduly the facilities for transporting, producing, manufacturing, supplying, storing or dealing in any article,
(b)	to prevent, limit or lessen, unduly, the manufacture or production of an article, or to enhance unreasonably the price thereof,
(c)	to prevent, or lessen, unduly, competition in the production, manufacture, purchase, barter, sale, storage, rental, transportation or supply of an article, or in the price of insurance upon persons or porperty, or

(d)	to restrain or injure trade or commerce in relation to any article,
is guilty of an indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for two years.
I emphasized the word "unduly", Mr. Speaker, because it appears in the first three paragraphs (a), (b) and (c). There have been many judicial interpretations of the first three clauses. The Supreme Court has stated that section 32 is designed to protect the public interest in free competition, and that it is a crime to conspire, combine, agree or arrange to unduly prevent or unduly lessen it. The statute proceeds upon the footing that the preventing or lessening of competition to the prohibited degree is in itself an injury to the public.
I do not know of any prosecution under paragraph (d) to which the proposed paragraph (e) is similar in thought and wording. In the first three paragraphs the word "unduly" is used, and this is a guideline for the courts. But under paragraph (d) there is no guideline and no words of limitation. The words are so wide as to be practically meaningless.
The proposed amendment, which if agreed to would be paragraph (e), appears to follow the thinking in paragraph (d) and simply states that to limit or restrain persons from participating in or observing sport to the detriment or against the interests of the public is an offence. A prosecution under this paragraph would indeed be most difficult, and I feel would not accomplish the result sought.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, as proposed paragraph (e) reads it is conceivable that a charge could be laid against a coach for benching a player or against a refereee for suspending a star player for two or three games, particularly if this occurred during a national play-off. Is that what we seek to have included?
In any event, Mr. Speaker, the proposal is out of step with the philosophy of the act. It does not deal with maintaining competition among employers of athletes as with other employers covered by the act, but rather seeks to protect the rights of people to participate in or observe a professional sport. Moreover, Mr. Speaker, if the act is to be widened to include services, as the Economic Council and director of investigation and research under the act may very well conclude, it may be that many other services should be covered,-I can think of many but I shall not name them-in which event all of these new sections should be drafted together
September 27, 1968	COMMONS
to conform with the over-all philosophy of the act.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, while I support what the mover and seconder of this bill and the earlier bill wish to do, I think it unwise to amend the act in this manner when it is most doubtful that it could bring about the desired result. The research that is going on will probably produce a far more effective and efficient procedure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this bill because my interest in it arises from the fact that it is an attempt to break open the combines act and to bring in a new type of offence or new type of matter which is not there now. As has been mentioned by other hon. members, the combines act presently covers offences relating to the sale of or trading in commodities; it does not deal with the sale of or trading in services.
For some time now I have supported movements to change the act to cover services. This bill is an attempt to amend the combines act to bring within its terms professional sport. While I support the thought and principle behind this attempt, I think it would be bad legislation if we amended an act such as this, or any other act, merely to bring in individual instances each time there was a complaint. This time it might be professional sports; another time it might be the laundry business or business consultants, and so on. A public service industry might be involved. I submit our legislation would be much improved if we amended the Combines Investigation Act to cover the sale of services as well as the sale of commodities.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
Some hon. members of the house and many members of the public wonder why it is an offence to restrain trade and fix prices with respect to the sale of commodities when it is not an offence to fix prices with respect to the sale of services. There seems to be no good reason for the distinction. Looking at the history of the act we see that when it was first passed the main problems related to trade in commodities and not to services. Then service businesses were operated under small proprietorships in local shops, and so on, and competition was intense. Now large syndicates are in the service industries. Appropriately, as mentioned in this bill, one must include all professional sports, which are very big business indeed.
DEBATES	539
Combines Investigation Act
I would be favourable to amending the Combines Investigation Act but I want the amendment to bring in not just professional sports but service industries generally, included in which are the professional sports industries.
We are told that the director of investigation and research for the combines department often receives complaints related to combines in service industries. Since his authority is limited, he has not been able to take action. In some instances where the applicability of the act is uncertain, that is, in gray areas, there have been actions before the courts in cases where services have been tied to the sale of commodities. For instance, there is the well known case of the Queen V. Beamish Construction, which went to the Ontario Court of Appeal. In this case different construction men combined together before submitting construction bids to the Government of Ontario, I believe. They were charged under the Combines Investigation Act and the Ontario Court of Appeal decided that since these men were to build something for the Ontario government they were combining to sell services; and the sale of services did not come under the act. Therefore, what happened was found to be not illegal.
There is also the case of the Queen V. Canadian Coat and Apron Supply, in which a company was charged with violating the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act in that it was restraining trade with respect to the supply of towels and laundry services to different businesses. That case was dismissed because the court found that the company performed a service; and service industries, even in instances where commodities were involved, were not covered by the act.
I think, therefore, that the act ought to be amended to cover service industries, since there may be a restraint of trade which involves services as well as commodities. I submit that this ought to be considered. As the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Chappell) said in his speech, the entire Combines Investigation Act and all pertinent combines legislation has been referred to the economic council for consideration and recommendation.
A major complaint against the Combines Investigation Act is that there is confusion in the minds of many about its true principle or purpose. Is the Combines Investigation Act designed to attain economic goals or is it principally criminal legislation? Many, including economists and experts in this field,
September 27, 1968

Combines Investigation Act feel that the Combines Investigation Act, in its concentration on restraints of trade, concentrates too much on the fact of combines rather than on what may be good for the economy. It has been suggested that we ought to decide whether a combine or a monopoly is good or bad for the country. In drafting or applying such legislation consideration ought also to be given to the state of employment in the economy, to the balance of payments, to the effect that any particular industry has on our foreign trade, to the formation of domestic capital, to the question of the ownership of Canadian industry and to regional development and economic planning. All those factors ought to be taken into consideration before we decide whether a combination or monopoly is illegal. The present act does not allow for these considerations.

I believe that now that the hon. gentleman is a minister and has responsibility for this legislation he would agree that it would be better to make provision for a broader amendment which would include all the service industries, among them, professional sport. In fact, I believe the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond would also approve of this suggestion. I notice he took up the exact wording used by

the minister when he drafted this bill; there was not much originality shown on his part. But he supports the principle, and I believe he would also support a broader amendment which would cover the service industry generally.
When I was interrupted I was discussing the need for an even more drastic amendment to the combines legislation because, as I have said, the present legislation does not consider the ultimate goal which a combines act is intended to achieve; it does not consider a situation in which combines and monopolies might be in the best interest of the economy. In Britain, in the common market countries and in Australia, changes have recently been made in the combines legislation to allow these factors to be taken into consideration. These countries have legislation similar to our own. Restraint of trade is illegal, but they do provide, now, for a situation in which the establishment of a monopoly might work to the benefit of the economy as a whole by speeding industrial growth, helping the employment situation, advancing foreign trade, and so on.
A number of studies have been made on this point including a most important one by V. W. Bladen and S. Stykolt who wrote a paper entitled "A Combines Policy in the Public Interest". They stated that the Canadian combines policy had paid too much attention to the form and too little to effects; that competition, as it had been interpreted by those administering the policy, had seemed to be an end in itself rather than a means to an end, that end being a well functioning economy delivering the maximum amount of goods and services at a minimum real cost.
In other words, what we need is a complete revision of this act, taking into consideration the part which combines might play in helping a society achieve its economic goals. The economic council has been asked about these things and we shall have to await a report. In the meantime, with respect to this bill, let me say I would support a measure which would include professional sport but that if we are to amend legislation as important as combines legislation we should not do so piecemeal but include an amendment which would cover all the service industries.

We have reached a point where professional sport, indeed all the service industries, should be made subject to combines legislation. This amendment is a good amendment but it does not go far enough. I am confident that the report of the economic council will propose that regulations be more far reaching than the type anticipated in this amendment. Professional sport in this country, now growing at a phenomenal rate, should be regarded in the same light as any other business enterprise. Cartels in professional sport are just as wrong as cartels which operate in restraint of trade and against the public interest in any other sector of the economy. Yet some of the professional promoters, particularly the hockey moguls in Canada today, attempt to suggest to us that their sole interest is to provide leisure-time entertainment for the working people of Canada and that profit is the furthest thought from their minds.
They claim they are not in business, that they are sportsmen, and that because they are sportsmen their activities in the area of professional hockey and football should not be made subject to the normal regulations which apply to industry in Canada. They say they are not in sport for money; they just want to provide lots of fun for Canadians on Saturday nights. And when it is suggested that they should be made the subject of investigation they throw up their hands in horror and say they are being dealt with unfairly and that they are victims of discrimination.
The plight of the hockey barons in Canada today is somewhat less tragic than the plight of little Eva hopping about on the ice floes. The National Hockey League is big business in every sense of the word. Last year Maple Leaf Gardens Corporation netted a profit of $900,706. In the six months ending February

These are interesting figures in relation to an industry which says it is not really in business at all. It is estimated that the philanthropic triumvirate made up of Stafford Smythe, Harold Ballard and John Bassett

I suggest there are many companies in Canada governed by combines legislation which failed to match this heady and scintillating performance. Yet we are told professional hockey is not big business in Canada.
Ask the people of Vancouver what they think about the N.H.L. and whether or not it is big business. Two years ago our great Canadian game of hockey pioneered new territories. It was expanded. It was not a case of "go west, young man." It was "go south to the United States, where the action is." Did Vancouver, or Calgary, or Winnipeg get a franchise? Were the Maritimes even considered? No! It was the "hot" hockey cities of Pittsburgh, St. Louis, Philadelphia, Oakland, Los Angeles and Minnesota which were awarded franchises. Vancouver, with the finest hockey arena in the world, seating over 15,000, was left out in the cold.

Forget about the fact that Vancouver is a great sports town. Forget about the fact that even with a somewhat indifferent football team we can fill Empire Stadium with 30,000 fans for every home game. Even forget about our history as a former Stanley Cup city, for indeed we were competing for the Stanley Cup at one time. Forget about our contributions in men and money to the national game of hockey. Forget all about that. The franchises went to the United States, to some centres where the fans could not care less, where they did not know what was taking place on the ice. Oakland, California, had 1,500 fans for one game, watching a listless team, in a centre filled with bewildered, dispirited people.
Why was Vancouver left out? Mr. Clarence Campbell and the directors of the N.H.L. said they did not think the quality of the Vancouver presentation was adequate. Mr. Speaker, the person who was going to help to run hockey in Vancouver was Foster Hewitt. But they said that he did not know enough about hockey. The fact is not that Vancouver lacked experienced management. The fact is that Mr. Stafford Smythe came to Vancouver and he wanted the people of Vancouver to give him, free of charge, a vast chunk of real estate in downtown Vancouver where he said he would
