erect a hockey stadium. He wanted, in effect, a licence to print money. He, was very upset at the ingratitude of the natives of British Columbia when we rejected his proposal.
More important, these sportsmen, these philanthropists of the N.H.L. did not want to split up the $2.5 million that they get each year from television rights. They did not want to divide it three ways with another Canadian club. More than that, Mr. Speaker, when they looked at the television possibilities of those United States "markets" they fairly drooled, and any suggestion that they wanted to advance Canada's national game in other Canadian centres went completely out the window.
What do these Canadian sports bosses want this year? There are record profits at the Gardens, and record profits at Montreal, but now they want $4 million for the television rights. They have not given any indication that they want to divide this money with new clubs in the Maritimes or with clubs in Vancouver, Winnipeg, Calgary, or any other centre. In Maple Leaf Gardens seat prices are going to be boosted again. This is not bad for an organization which says it is in a nonprofit business, that it is not really in business at all, that it is really 'just there to please folks". British Columbia has been patted on the head. They say that if we stand in line, if we watch our P's and Q's and if we are loyal to N.H.L. standards then, when they expand again, we just might get a franchise. I tell you this, Mr. Speaker, the people in western Canada are not holding their breaths.
Then, there are some people who say that this is a business which should not be regulated. What about players' contracts? Here again the N.H.L. is riddled with restrictions on freedom. Where else in the world would you find a situation where a hockey player, when he decides to retire, cannot find work in any other hockey organization, even upstairs sweeping the floor, unless he gets permission from his former owners?
Take the case of Red Kelly, a former member of this house. What happened to Red? You read about it. Most of you sports fans know. He retired from the Leafs and wanted to coach the Los Angeles Kings. The Leafs management told him, "You cannot get that job with the Los Angeles Kings unless we make a deal with the Los Angeles club." The fact is that under the feudal sports baronies established in the National Hockey League, Red Kelly couldn't sell popcorn for the Los Angeles Kings unless he got the approval of Stafford Smythe and his pals.

There are still some people in Canada who want to defend the status quo. They say it is the same all over the world. It is not, Mr. Speaker. Take the case of the Baltimore Colts' Ray Berry, an outstanding player fqr the Baltimore team. The day he retired he was hired by the Dallas Cowboys as end coach. He had his new job the following day. There were no deals, no feudal property rights involved. He was a free man. In England soccer players are often sold by their clubs. "Transfer" is the word they use in England, and the price may go up to $300,000. What happens when a player is transferred from one team to another in Britain where they are very zealous about the protection of human rights and freedoms? The player is called in and asked if he wants to be transferred. If he says yes he gets a percentage of the transfer fee. In Canada, if an N.H.L. player does not report to the club to which he has been sold then that is the last time he puts on skates in Canada or anywhere else.
How long are we going to tolerate a situation like this in Canada, let alone the matter of the profits? The Profits which are being gathered by these organizations are not subject to regulations affecting normal business. Some sports writers have said that N.H.L. players are well paid. Some of them are, but others of real talent are languishing in the minors, caught in that feudal web where their rights are restricted, a web which prevents some of them from making the N.H.L. with some other team. Clubs should not be able to send players to the minors if other N.H.L. clubs can use them.
I believe that players should be tied to specific clubs only for the length of their contracts instead of being the lifetime property of the clubs with which they sign. In any other business, and hockey is big business, if an employee works with a major company and fulfils his obligation to that company, he can go to work in an ancillary field. Why are civil rights denied to so many of our professional athletes?
Professional sport must be placed under federal regulation, but this should go beyond

professional sports. It should also apply to service industries, and we should make sure that the kind of legislation which we pass in the House of Commons is going to be air tight, is going to be water tight, that it is not going to be possible for some of these professional sports promoters, making millions of dollars as they do each year, to find a loophole through which they can drive wedges to the detriment of the public. The sooner this is done the better, especially in view of the substantial increase in leisure time which will result in expansion of professional sports of all kinds.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the Combines Investigation Act must be amended to provide that those who conspire to combine, to limit, or restrict the opportunity in Canada of persons to participate in or observe any professional sport, and which operate against the public interest, shall be guilty of an offence and appropriate action taken. I look forward to the recommendations which will come from the economic council, and let us hope the government acts on a broad scale, not on the worthy but limited scale suggested in this bill.
